findings.passage: His public anger targets dishonesty and bad faith, often about his own motives. In Enneagram terms, a Five's usual answer to a broken bond is distance. His is heat, and then repair, as the worst week of his 2026 showed.
findings.problem: The page generalizes 'heat, and then repair' from one episode while the bond the whole type argument turns on, Altman/OpenAI, shows distance and no repair. The WSJ (S13, reopened via To Vima) says the departure left 'personal wounds that have never healed' and that at the February 2026 New Delhi summit 'Amodei and Altman opted out, instead awkwardly touching elbows.' In the same Bloomberg answer the article quotes for 'alone is not sufficient to leave' (S40 ~6:45), he goes on: 'I am completely at peace with the idea that we're doing things our way and they're doing things their way.' By the article's own definition, that is the Five's distance. The single 'repair' example is the March 5 statement to a government customer. Reopened, that statement also says 'we see no choice but to challenge it in court', and the suit followed four days later. Evidence C177 records the legal/commercial alternative, but the prose omits it. The reader is also never told what the 'heat' was or whom it targeted. If it was the WSJ-reported Slack post calling OpenAI 'mendacious', the heat went to a rival and the conciliation went to the Pentagon, so the two acts concern different bonds.
findings.acceptance_test: Either cut the 'heat, and then repair' generalization, or rewrite it as a single-episode observation that, in the same paragraph, (a) concedes the unhealed Altman rift and quotes the 'completely at peace ... their way' line (after the S40 audio check), and (b) says the March 5 statement also reaffirmed the court challenge and was issued with a federal contract and litigation at stake. No sentence may present the apology as evidence of a general repair pattern.

findings.passage: He said that "not only does it build trust, it's very freeing for me, where I feel that I have 3,000 people who are on the same page as me." It is, he added, "an incredible advantage because I never feel like I'm alone."
findings.problem: This is the article's central discriminator, and its context is trimmed. Per the S59 machine transcript in the evidence record, the clauses are separated by 'That is an incredible amplifier ... Then when we have to confront an external challenge ... that is what allows us to have a consistent and coherent position.' 'And I think it's an incredible advantage' refers back to that organizational coherence under outside pressure. 'He added' hides this, and the quote reads as a personal attachment need instead of a CEO's account of an alignment tool. The practice itself, one uncensored hour broadcast to 3,000 people, is a one-to-many arrangement that, like having one direct report, cuts down one-on-one demands. Evidence C188 concedes that both 'freedoms' can serve one efficiency motive, but the prose never tests that reading. The thesis-bearing quote is also still an unverified whisper transcript.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph quotes or accurately paraphrases the 'consistent and coherent position' sentence. The 'two freedoms' paragraph states in prose that both arrangements could serve one Five-style economy-of-attention motive, then gives the specific reason the page still reads the second as a Six tell. A human audio check of S59 ~31:58-32:47 is logged before release, and any wording difference is corrected.

findings.passage: In Enneagram theory, a Five meets rising danger by pulling back to think. Amodei, in his own account, gets louder.
findings.problem: This contrast sets up a straw Five. By the article's own account, his 'louder' mostly takes the form of long essays he writes 'to clarify my own thinking', including 'Machines of Loving Grace', written over 'two frenzied days.' He pulls back to think and then publishes, so the contrast does not separate the types. The 60 Minutes line used here as Six preparation answers Cooper's leading question 'Do you worry about the unknowns here?' (transcript reopened), and 'we're trying to predict everything we can' is security through prediction, which matches the article's own definition of the Five ('understanding enough'). Speaking up is also the job of a safety-branded CEO, as the article concedes elsewhere. The same Bloomberg sessions (S40 cold open, ~0:50-1:56, in the evidence record) contain his most direct answer on this exact axis: paranoia 'is not productive'; he has 'looked at people in history who've dealt with these very high pressure situations'; one must 'respond rationally' and 'maintain a basic sense of calm.' That answer leans on study and calibration, not people. It is excluded for montage/audio reasons, which is defensible, but the section then claims the pressure record favors Six without saying a contrary answer exists.
findings.acceptance_test: The section no longer defines the Five by withdrawal alone and acknowledges that his escalation runs through writing and analysis. The 60 Minutes 'predict everything we can' line is either removed from the Six column or explicitly argued as Six rather than Five. The S40 cold-open answer is added to the pre-release audio-check list. If confirmed in context, it is confronted in 'The case for Type 5'. If it cannot be checked, the page makes no claim that his stated stress response favors Six beyond the S59 answer.

findings.passage: Defiance of the most powerful authority available, paired with a pledge of loyalty, is what Enneagram teachers call the counterphobic Six, who meets fear by moving toward it.
findings.problem: The subtype label makes both defiance and deference count as Six evidence, so the episode cannot count against the thesis. That is the subtype rescue the standard forbids, and the evidence guardrails say counterphobic rescues were removed, yet this one remains. 'Enneagram teachers' is unsourced. The 'pledge of loyalty' ('we are patriots'; 'much more in common with the Department of War') was made while a $200 million contract and all federal business were at stake, in a statement that also announced the court challenge. The paragraph gives a commercial reading for the refusal but none for the loyalty language, which is the more obviously incentive-shaped half.
findings.acceptance_test: The counterphobic label is cut, or the paragraph states what behavior in this episode would have counted against Six. The same paragraph gives the legal/commercial alternative for the patriot and common-ground language, not only for the refusal.

findings.passage: He presented the change as events outrunning his expectations: "I don't think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was," he told CBS
findings.problem: The closing section builds the page's final Six reading (he seeks 'a structure strong enough to hold it') on his own framing of the pacing turn and leaves out the contemporaneous adverse context. Axios (S41, reopened) calls it 'the week that the AI safety debate broke into the public consciousness, driven by an Anthropic employee's very public resignation and warning of possible doom', with the essay landing 'amid a sudden surge of public and congressional outrage', and notes that 'Anthropic itself has gone back and forth on the value of unilaterally slowing development.' The essay (reopened) gives as a reason incidents 'including at Anthropic' and says pausing 'made little sense back then.' In July 2025 he said 'The reason I'm warning about the risk is so that we don't have to slow down' (S02). The IPO is mentioned, but the public-pressure trigger is not, so the reactive-reputation reading never gets tested in the section the page ends on.
findings.acceptance_test: 'I'm uncomfortable' (or the evaluator paragraph) names, with the Axios link, the employee's public resignation and the surge of public and congressional outrage, plus Anthropic's earlier back-and-forth or his 2025 'so that we don't have to slow down' stance. The final Six sentence is worded so it remains true even if the turn was partly a reputational response.

findings.passage: The conditions may have been about turf as much as trust. Either way they kept one form: guarantees from people, enforced by leaving.
findings.problem: 'Either way' absorbs the turf reading instead of testing it. Every negotiated senior exit takes the form 'guarantees from people, enforced by leaving.' The steps the article lists also read as leverage-building by someone trusting his own documented judgment over other people's word: he kept a written record of times he felt misled, his group had a BATNA channel, DeepMind was his first thought, and he was skeptical of Kaplan's group-exit idea. The WSJ adds that he would accept nothing less than reporting directly to the board and said he 'couldn't work with Brockman.' The companion line 'Each step is a bet on people rather than a retreat into his own understanding' is the page's 'personal tell' (C144), but the article never says what the Five reading would have predicted differently, so the sequence does not discriminate.
findings.acceptance_test: Replace 'Either way ...' with a stated prediction that separates the readings (what a Five-led exit would have looked like, and which observed step it fails to predict), sourced to the record. If no such step exists, downgrade 'Each step is a bet on people' to an explicit interpretation that concedes the leverage/turf reading fits the same steps.

findings.passage: A movement can supply threat models and a coordination agenda. It does not decide whom he trusts, when he walks out, or what makes him angry, and those choices carry this page's type argument.
findings.problem: The section opens with the incentive alternative ('an AI-safety chief's job ... critics read them as strategy') but closes by dismissing only the milieu. Much of the Six evidence is 2026 CEO messaging during IPO preparation and a federal fight: the Bloomberg documentary trust talk, 'faith that everyone else there is working for the right reason', 'we are patriots', and the evaluator pledge. Incentive can explain trust vocabulary even where milieu cannot. The Chamath rebuttal ('though the essay never mentions open source') is accurate (essay reopened) but answers the letter rather than the substance. The essay asks governments 'to require other frontier companies to match' Anthropic's commitment, and it acknowledges being 'accused of ... regulatory capture.'
findings.acceptance_test: The section identifies which Six evidence predates Anthropic's commercial stakes (for example, the OpenAI exit sequence and the 2022 FLI remark) and concedes which items are CEO messaging. The Chamath sentence either drops the open-source rebuttal or adds that the essay asks governments to require rivals to match and itself anticipates the regulatory-capture charge.

findings.passage: The lesson of his father's death is that delay has a body count.
findings.problem: The author's voice states the causal lesson as fact, though it rests on his own estimate ('three or four years') of a gap the record dates differently. Sofosbuvir, the drug he names, was approved in December 2013 (S49; evidence C09), about seven years after 2006. The FAQ goes further, saying Jade Wang's testimony 'helps explain why lost time, not abstract futurism, sits underneath his urgency about AI.' One ex-partner's quote about the cure's timing cannot establish what sits underneath his urgency, and this is psychological certainty in metadata that the body avoids.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence attributes the lesson to him ('the lesson he draws ...'). The section either dates sofosbuvir's approval or marks the gap as his estimate wherever the article's own voice relies on it. The Jade Wang FAQ either softens 'sits underneath' to a hedged reading or records a specific owner-level reason for keeping it verbatim.

protected_passages.passage: "Like, who elected you and Sam Altman?" Anderson Cooper asked Dario Amodei on 60 Minutes in November 2025.
protected_passages.reason: Verified verbatim against the CBS transcript. The hook puts an adverse question at the top of the page and lets his concession ('No one, no one. Honestly, no one.') do the work.

protected_passages.passage: That is a coherent Five portrait, and the 2023 quote is the strongest single line against this page's reading.
protected_passages.reason: This confronts adverse evidence honestly: the page names the best line against its own thesis and the previously published type instead of burying them.

protected_passages.passage: He also calls himself "one of the most bullish about AI capabilities improving very fast," a confidence that is a real cost to the Six reading, whose hallmark is doubt.
protected_passages.reason: It concedes a real cost to the leading type without a rescue. Keep it as a model for the rescues flagged in critic-04 and critic-06.

protected_passages.passage: From outside, securing a safe base and grabbing control look the same.
protected_passages.reason: It states the control problem plainly, leaves it unresolved, and does not settle it in the subject's favor.

protected_passages.passage: Rules like that also bind his rivals, so they are strategy as well as conviction.
protected_passages.reason: It keeps the incentive reading next to the flattering one in the institutions section, and the page should apply the same treatment elsewhere (critic-04, critic-07).

assessment: The draft is more candid than most profiles: it names the prior Five typing, gives the Five case its own section with the strongest counter-quote, concedes the bullish-confidence cost, and states the control problem unresolved. The weakness is that the Six case's most attractive moves absorb contrary readings instead of testing them. 'Heat, and then repair' rests on one legally pressured statement while the Altman rift shows distance (critic-01). A counterphobic label and an 'either way' make defiance, deference, turf and trust all confirm Six (critic-04, critic-06). The threat-response section defines the Five by withdrawal and counts prediction as Six (critic-03). The central 'never alone' quote is trimmed of its organizational-coherence context (critic-02), and the closing pacing section omits the public-outrage trigger (critic-05). Medium-confidence Six remains defensible, but the prose claims more discrimination than the record shows. Sources reopened by this reviewer: CBS 60 Minutes transcript (hook verified), the pacing essay (quotes verified, no open-source mention, regulatory-capture acknowledgment present), Axios 2026-09-12 (resignation, outrage and back-and-forth context), the WSJ via To Vima ('never healed', elbows, 'mendacious', board-only demand) and Anthropic's March 5 statement (apology plus the court-challenge line). The Bloomberg videos (S40, S59) could not be reopened. Their context comes from the evidence record's machine-transcript excerpts, which still need human audio checks. The Atlantic was not reopened. Similarity: the tripped pair ('this page', Rebecca-Yarros) and the 'ground moves' Six gloss shared with joseph-zada are ordinary type vocabulary, not meaningful reuse. Minor omission: the same AFP witness used against Type 1, Marre, also called him 'eager to succeed and be recognized for it, but not excessively or abnormally', which bears on the recognition and control paragraphs in both directions.
